name: Kira Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My week is full of bodies, basically. Anatomy lectures with the skeleton model we've named Gerald, a practical session where we learn to find muscles by touch, and volleyball training twice a week with the university team. I live in a flat with four others on the third floor, which means lots of stairs and lots of complaining. On Sundays I help my parents at their garden centre for a few hours, which is how I got used to being on my feet all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably a bit of both, some useful bits and some hype, and we'll see. I wouldn't post anything online, because I try to stay out of arguments. I'd tell my friends to use whatever helps them study and not to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel fine. Physiotherapy is a hands-on job and demand keeps growing as people get older. I'd just keep studying and hope my results hold up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: lectures, practicals, volleyball, Sunday shifts at the garden centre. I'd apply for a hospital volunteering placement over the summer, to see different physiotherapy settings. I'd also start looking at which specialities, like sports or older people's care, appeal to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. My parents cover everything, and there's a growing need for physiotherapists, so I feel I picked well. I'd have the odd exam panic, but that's normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd carry on. What would you still worry about in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the NHS-style waiting lists. My grandmother waited months for a knee appointment, so I'd be walking into an overloaded system, and a plateau doesn't fix that. I think about it more than I think about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your volleyball team feel about this stuff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd roll their eyes. We use a scheduling app for training and it keeps double-booking the sports hall, so nobody on the team thinks AI is scary yet. We're more worried about the next match.

say: I'd say it's **a bit of both**, some useful, some hype, and we'll see.
I'd tell friends to use whatever helps them **study**.
think: Privately I'd feel **fine**, since demand for physiotherapy keeps growing.
I think more about **waiting lists** than about AI.
do: Keep up lectures, practicals, volleyball and **Sunday shifts** at the garden centre.
Apply for a summer **hospital volunteering** placement.
feel: **Calm**, since my parents cover costs and demand for physios is growing.
S0.quote: My grandmother waited months for a knee appointment, so I'd be walking into an overloaded system, and a plateau doesn't fix that.
fieldNote: Her worry is **overloaded health services**, which she sees through her grandmother.
She avoids **online arguments**, a steady and private style.
Calm rests on **rising demand** and family money.

steps.text: Apply for a summer hospital volunteering placement
Look at sports and older-people's physiotherapy as a speciality
Wait and see how my university adds new tools before changing study habits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it will change the paperwork a lot, and the clinical side much less. I'd tell the first-years in my team that it's worth learning one or two tools now, because everyone will be expected to. I'd say it quietly, since I'm not an influencer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I feel steady. The notes, booking and referral letters are the first things to go, which could free up physios to spend longer with patients. If hospitals instead cut physio posts to save money, I'd be less relaxed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using AI a bit more for writing and revision, and ask my placement supervisors which software they use. I'd take an optional module on health technology if there is one. I'd also keep up my practical skills, because that's what I'd really sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a note of caution. I think my field is better placed than most, and I know that, but I'd keep an eye on what hospitals actually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of physiotherapy do you think software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The notes and letters, and the first assessment of a patient, like an app that suggests exercises. I'd happily lose the writing of notes and letters, because a physio spends about a third of the day on it and I'd rather spend that time with patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel if your lecturers used AI to mark your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine if the marking was fair and someone checked it. A person's judgement still matters. I'd ask my lecturer to explain how it works, and I think most of them would, because they're quite open.

say: I'd say the **paperwork** will change a lot and the clinical side much less.
I'd tell first-years to learn **one or two tools** now.
think: Privately I feel **steady**: notes and letters go first, freeing time for patients.
I'd be less relaxed if hospitals **cut physio posts** to save money.
do: Use AI a bit more for **revision** and ask supervisors which software they use.
Take an optional **health technology** module and keep practical skills sharp.
feel: **Calm with caution**, because my field is better placed than most.
S1.quote: I'd happily lose the writing of notes and letters, because a physio spends about a third of the day on it and I'd rather spend that time with patients.
fieldNote: She welcomes **paperwork loss**, which she sees as time freed for patients.
Her view of marking is **fairness-based**: checked and open.
She places **practical skill** as the thing she would sell.

steps.text: Use AI for revision and ask placement supervisors which software they use
Take an optional health technology module
Keep practising hands-on techniques in practicals and volunteering

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need clear plans fast, and that hospitals and universities should be talking to students now. I'd ask my course leader what the department's plan is. I'd also tell my team we should keep playing volleyball and look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be scared. Two years is nothing: I'd be in second year when thinking AI can do most desk work, and I'd be about to graduate into a world with no rule book. The hands-on part would get about three more years, which is comforting but not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying, because physiotherapy is hands-on and I'd be getting the skills that last longest. I'd ask the hospitals about the parts of the work that will change first, and try to specialise in something people will always want, like rehab after injury. I'd talk to my parents about savings and about the garden centre as a back-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I think, more than panicked. I'd feel the pressure and I'd be quieter than usual, but I'd also feel I had a decent answer in my pocket. I'd say it's like waiting for a big match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years: what does physiotherapy look like in your head then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that the work is more physical, a person is getting one of the most human jobs, and that this is a good time to be in it. And then I'd also say I'm a bit scared, because I couldn't stand pretending. Somebody has to put a hand on the sore shoulder and decide how hard to push, and I can't see that being a download. They'd listen better than I expect.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A busy ward, but with software doing the notes and the scheduling, and more waiting lists because everyone is losing other jobs. I'd imagine fewer new physios being hired at first, because hospitals are cautious with money. That's the bit I can't plan around.

say: I'd say we need **clear plans fast**, and students should be included now.
I'd ask my course leader what the **department's plan** is.
think: Privately I'd be **scared**: two years is nothing for what I'm training for.
Three more years for hands-on work is **comforting**, but not a plan.
do: Keep studying hands-on skills and aim at **rehab after injury**.
Talk to my parents about **savings** and the garden centre as a back-up.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than panicked, like waiting for a big match.
S2.quote: The hands-on part would get about three more years, which is comforting but not a plan.
fieldNote: Her **hands-on edge** helps, but she says openly that it is not a plan.
The **garden centre** is her family back-up, a concrete detail.
She plans to tell her parents **honestly** that she is scared.

steps.text: Ask hospitals which physiotherapy tasks change first and choose rehab after injury
Talk with my parents about savings and the garden centre as a back-up
Save more of my allowance each month
Ask my course leader what the department plans for students

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have enough time to adapt if we start now, and that the health service should be planning its workforce, not just waiting. I'd ask at the next student-staff meeting what they're doing. I'd keep it polite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be uneasy but hopeful. I'd graduate in about three years, and have a couple of years of practice before robots reach the hands-on work in 2034. That's a head start, but I wouldn't rely on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and add a postgraduate course in something specialised, like neurological rehab. I'd use AI tools a bit more for admin and revision, once I trust them. I'd also save a little each month from my Sunday pay, to have a cushion of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like looking at a long road with a bend you can't see round. I'd enjoy my degree more than I would with two years, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years: how do you use the time compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. Once enough people around me use it every day, I'd join in, because it would be silly not to. That's how I've always done it: wait, watch, then go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you feel differently about using AI every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: keep your hands-on skills sharp, make friends in other professions, and don't sit still. Contacts matter more than people think. A person who knows you will give you a chance before a form will, so I'd make friends in other professions and not sit still.

say: I'd say we have **enough time** if the health service plans its workforce.
I'd raise it politely at the **student-staff meeting**.
think: Privately I'm **uneasy but hopeful**, with about two years of practice before robots reach the work.
I wouldn't rely on that **head start**.
do: Add a **postgraduate course** in neurological rehab after the degree.
Save a little each month from **Sunday pay** for my own cushion.
feel: **Uneasy**, like looking down a road with an unseen bend.
S3.quote: A person who knows you will give you a chance before a form will, so I'd make friends in other professions and not sit still.
fieldNote: She values **contacts** over credentials, a practical view.
Her **wait, watch, then join** habit shows steady adaptability.
The head start from hands-on work is **recognised but not trusted**.

steps.text: Plan a postgraduate course in neurological rehab
Save a little from my Sunday garden centre pay every month
Start using AI for admin and revision once friends say it works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that ten years is enough time to get it right, and we should plan sensibly. I'd say the same about the health service: set aside money for training. I'd keep an eye on how colleagues do before I do anything bold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm pretty calm. By the end of ten years I'd be 29, a few years into a physiotherapy career, with robots just arriving. I'd feel I had time to find my niche, and my family would be there if I needed help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, work on a ward and in a sports clinic, and learn the AI tools as they mature. I'd also keep volleyball and friends close, because those are what keep me steady. I'd perhaps train as a coach too, as a side income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A tiny bit of worry in the background, like a phone left on silent. I'd get on with my life and check it now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, does the future feel like someone else's problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, honestly. When ten years is the horizon, it's easy to say someone else will sort it out. But I think I'm the kind of person who prepares quietly, and that's enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who is panicking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, take a deep breath, make a short list of what you can do this year, and do it. A list of three things beats a worry about everything, and then go and play something, whatever it is.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough time if we plan sensibly.
I'd say the health service should **set aside money** for training.
think: Privately I'm **calm**: I'd be 29, a few years into my career.
I'd have time to find my **niche**, with family to lean on.
do: Work on a ward and in a **sports clinic**, and learn AI tools as they mature.
Train as a **volleyball coach** for side income.
feel: **Calm**, with a faint worry like a phone left on silent.
S4.quote: A list of three things beats a worry about everything, and then go and play something, whatever it is.
fieldNote: She admits the long date makes it **easy to defer** to others.
Her advice to friends is **practical and short**.
The coaching idea shows **modest side-income thinking**.

steps.text: Work on a ward and in a sports clinic after qualifying
Train as a volleyball coach for extra income
Learn new AI tools once colleagues have used them for a while

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, I think, because physiotherapy needs years of practice on real people, and I'd have barely started. What would help is clear, honest information from the people who run health services about which jobs change and when. And some kind of fund that helps people retrain without going into debt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say I use AI sometimes, mostly to explain things I missed or to check my essay structure. I don't love it, but I don't hate it either. I tend to wait until my friends have tried something and it works, and then I join in.

headlineQuote: Somebody has to put a hand on the sore shoulder and decide how hard to push, and I can't see that being a download.
portrait: Kira is 19, studying **physiotherapy** with top results, a strong family cushion and a volleyball team.
She is centrist and steady: she uses AI **now and then** and adopts tools once friends have proved them.
She sees **hands-on care** as a protection, but not a complete one, and worries about the pace of change.
Her mood moves from calm to uneasy as **time shortens**, with a spike of worry when she thinks of the two-year case.
Her parents, her team and her flatmates are her support, and she would act by retraining and talking.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries her most, because physiotherapy needs years of practice she has barely started.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear, honest information** from health services about which jobs change and when.
A **retraining fund** that doesn't push people into debt.
